issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: 'Survival guilt' is hard to reconcile with a stalking trauma in the absence of any indication that other people died or were put at comparable lethal risk. For this trauma type, that appraisal is clinically implausible rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
issues.explanation: A specific taste trigger is not impossible, but for stalking it lacks support from the rest of the profile: there are no memory items or contextual details suggesting an event involving gustatory cues. Given the formulation also has no Triggers ↔ Memory linkage, this trigger is clinically unsupported and difficult to explain in this profile.

vignette:
Eric is a 32-year-old tutor who works one-on-one with students in his home office. The stalking began quietly: a student named Kevin started staying after sessions to talk, then began sending long emails, then waiting outside the building. One evening, Kevin cornered Eric in the parking lot, his face twisted with anger as he shouted accusations. Then he revved his motorcycle and sped away, leaving the engine noise ringing in Eric’s ears. That was the last time Eric saw him, but the sound of a motorcycle or the sight of someone following too closely on the street now makes his stomach drop. Each time he hears an angry voice—even a colleague’s calm frustration—his mind snaps back to that moment, and the old thought surfaces: I should have seen this coming. I can’t trust myself to know who people really are. This self-doubt has become a constant companion, feeding a broader certainty that people are not what they seem and that everyone carries a hidden threat.

Because Eric has come to believe that he cannot judge others accurately, he has begun to avoid situations where he would have to let his guard down. He tells himself he deserves the isolation—that he should have been more careful, that suffering is what he gets for being naive. So he avoids emotional closeness with his wife, staying late at the desk or going to bed after she is asleep. He also avoids relaxing, because stillness feels exposed; if he lets his mind wander, danger might creep in. These habits feel like penance, but they also keep him constantly vigilant. At night, the same hypervigilance wakes him several times, barely audible sounds pulling him upright. He often startles at nothing—a creak in the house, a car outside—and his heart hammers as if Kevin were in the room again. These false alarms convince him that danger is imminent, and that feeling of being unsafe sends him scanning his environment all over again. The more he scans, the more he misinterprets ordinary events: a neighbor walking behind him on the sidewalk becomes someone following him; the rumble of a truck sounds like a motorcycle. Each misinterpretation then confirms his distrust of people and his own judgment.

At work, Eric now refuses to meet new students at unfamiliar coffee shops or libraries. He insists that they come to his home, where he can control the exits. Yet even there, he cannot relax: last week a student raised his voice in excitement over a test score, and Eric froze, seeing anger where there was none. He ended the session early and spent the evening ruminating—punishing himself for overreacting, but also for not trusting his own instincts. The cycle tightens: his avoidance of unfamiliar places reinforces his belief that the world is dangerous; his belief that people cannot be trusted makes him avoid intimacy; and the growing exhaustion from broken sleep only sharpens his false alarms. He has stopped going to the grocery store alone, and his wife has noticed how he flinches when she touches his shoulder from behind. She has asked him to talk to someone, but he tells her he deserves to feel this way.

What finally brought Eric to therapy was a morning when he could not bring himself to unlock the front door for a scheduled tutoring session. He stood in the hallway, sweating, convinced that the student had been sent by Kevin to confront him. He knew it was not rational, but the fear was absolute. Now he sits in the office and says he wants to stop living in a world where every person and every sound feels like a trap. He hopes that someone can show him how to trust again—but he is terrified that if he lets his guard down, he will only prove that he never should have.
